t: Why a Headlamp Beats a Flashlight for PC Building
title: Why a Headlamp Beats a Flashlight for PC Building
description: PC building is two-handed work in dark corners — front-panel headers, EPS connectors behind the cooler, screws under the shroud. A headlamp puts the light where you look, hands-free, while a flashlight needs a hand you do not have or a mouth you should not use. Once you build with a headlamp, going back to a flashlight feels like working blind.

demo.program:
print("PC building: 2 hands busy + dark corners (headers, EPS, under shroud).")
print("Headlamp: light follows your eyes, hands free.")
print("Flashlight: needs a hand you don't have.")
print("Build once with a headlamp: flashlights feel like working blind after.")

t: Lumens, Beam Patterns, and What PC Work Needs
title: Lumens, Beam Patterns, and What PC Work Needs
description: Case interiors need 100 to 300 lumens — enough to read tiny silkscreen labels, not so much that reflections blind you off the side panel. A flood beam (wide, even) beats a spot beam inside a case; spots are for across-the-room. Adjustable brightness matters more than max lumens: low for close board work, high for peering into the PSU basement.

demo.program:
print("Need: 100-300 lm (read silkscreen, no blinding reflections).")
print("Flood > spot inside a case (even light, no harsh hotspot).")
print("Adjustable brightness > max lumens: low for boards, high for deep corners.")

title: Battery Types: Rechargeable vs Disposable
description: Rechargeable headlamps (USB-C, built-in cell) cost more upfront and are always ready if you keep them charged; AAA headlamps run on cheap cells you can swap mid-job but eat batteries. For bench use, rechargeable wins — the lamp lives on the bench charger. For the go-bag, AAA wins — a spare set of cells weighs nothing and never needs a wall outlet.

demo.program:
print("Rechargeable (USB-C): bench king, always ready on its charger.")
print("AAA: go-bag king, spare cells weigh nothing, no outlet needed.")
print("Bench = rechargeable. Go-bag = AAA. Match power to context.")

t: Comfort: Weight, Straps, and Long Sessions
title: Comfort: Weight, Straps, and Long Sessions
description: A headlamp you will not wear is useless. Under 3 ounces (85 g) with a balanced battery, a wide elastic strap that does not pinch, and a tilt hinge that holds its angle — those are the comfort specs. Top straps add stability for active work but annoy at the bench; skip them for PC use. If it hurts after an hour, it stays in the drawer.

demo.program:
print("Comfort specs: <3 oz, balanced, wide non-pinching strap, tilt hinge that holds.")
print("Top strap: skip for bench use (annoys more than it stabilizes).")
print("Hurts after an hour = stays in drawer = useless. Comfort IS the spec.")

t: Use Case: Front-Panel Headers and Tiny Labels
title: Use Case: Front-Panel Headers and Tiny Labels
description: Front-panel headers are the headlamp's signature job: tiny pins, tinier silkscreen labels (+/- markings you cannot read in case shadow), in the darkest corner of the case. Headlamp on low flood, tilt the beam straight down the header row, and the labels read clearly. This single task justifies the headlamp for most builders.

t: Use Case: Reading Serial Numbers and Inspecting Boards
title: Use Case: Reading Serial Numbers and Inspecting Boards
description: Warranty claims need serial numbers from dark corners; board inspection needs raking light across the surface to spot bulging capacitors or scorch marks. Tilt the headlamp low across the board — defects cast shadows and pop out. For serials, the flood beam plus a phone camera reads labels your eyes cannot quite resolve.

t: Red-Light and Low Modes: When Less Light Is More
title: Red-Light and Low Modes: When Less Light Is More
description: Red modes preserve night vision for late builds and will not blast your eyes off a reflective side panel; low white modes do close work without glare. Avoid strobe/SOS modes near the bench — they are useless for building and annoying to everyone. The modes you need: high, medium, low, red. Everything else is marketing.

demo.program:
print("Red: night vision + no panel-blast reflections.")
print("Low white: close board work without glare.")
print("Need: high/medium/low/red. Strobe: useless at the bench.")

t: Water Resistance and Build Quality Ratings
title: Water Resistance and Build Quality Ratings
description: IPX4 (splash-resistant) is plenty for bench and field PC work — it survives rain on a site visit. IPX7 (submersion) is overkill unless you build PCs on boats. More important than the rating: the tilt hinge should survive thousands of adjustments and the battery door should latch positively. A dead hinge makes the lamp a neck-worn flashlight.

demo.program:
print("IPX4: enough (site-visit rain). IPX7: overkill (unless boats).")
print("Matter more: hinge survives 1000s of tilts, battery door latches positive.")
print("Dead hinge = lamp becomes a neck-worn flashlight.")

t: Maintenance: Charging Discipline and Strap Care
title: Maintenance: Charging Discipline and Strap Care
description: Rechargeables die when forgotten: dock the bench lamp after every session so it is always ready. Wash the elastic strap occasionally — sweat and dust make it slip. Check the tilt hinge yearly; a drop of silicone keeps it smooth. For AAA lamps, remove cells during long storage to prevent leakage damage.

demo.program:
print("Rechargeable: dock after EVERY session (forgotten = dead when needed).")
print("Wash strap (sweat slips). Yearly: hinge check + silicone drop.")
print("AAA: remove cells in long storage (leakage kills lamps).")

t: Headlamp vs Magnetic Work Light vs Phone Light

Phone light: always with you, one hand lost, awkward angles — emergency only. The bench wants a headlamp first; a magnetic area light second; the phone stays a backup.

title: Buying Guide: The $25 Sweet Spot
description: The sweet spot is around 25 dollars: 200-300 lumens, flood beam, USB-C rechargeable, tilt hinge, under 3 ounces, IPX4. Below 15 dollars you get weak beams and hinges that die in months; above 50 buys features (gesture sensors, huge lumens) that PC work does not need. Try the strap fit before committing — comfort is personal.

title: Advanced: Lighting for Build Photography
description: Documenting builds needs even light: headlamp on medium flood for the work area plus a magnetic work light bounced off the ceiling for fill. t: Technique: The Scan Pattern for Final Inspection
title: Technique: The Scan Pattern for Final Inspection
description: Before the side panel closes, run the scan: headlamp on medium, slow sweep across every connector (seated? latched?), every fan (clear of cables?), every screw zone (all screws in?), and the board surface (stray screws? tools left inside?). Two minutes of lit inspection catches the forgotten EPS cable and the screwdriver still in the case.

demo.program:
scan = ["connectors seated + latched?", "fans clear of cables?",
        "all screws placed?", "board: stray screws/tools?"]
print("Pre-close scan (medium flood, slow sweep):")
for s in scan:
    print(f"  ? {s}")
print("2 minutes catches the forgotten EPS cable and the screwdriver inside.")
